Genetically engineered Natural Killer Cells – a new tool for cancer immunotherapy (NKImmunoTher)

Contact us

The project

Abstract

Background: Metastasis is the leading cause of cancer mortality and it is needed much effort to manage this discouraged disease. The innate ability of NK cells to eliminate cancer cells made them a best candidate for cancer immunotherapy, NK cell-based immunotherapies against cancer have been investigated for years. The development and progression of cancer is shaped by tumor and host immune system cross-talk, a number of mechanisms contribute to cell immune suppression. One of the most important mechanisms is the production of inhibitory cytokines such as transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β). This cytokine can strongly affect the activity of NK cells, reducing the cytotoxic capacity of these cells and impairing their antitumor activity. Blocking or lacking of TGF-β receptor 2 (TGFBR2) on NK cells can restore the cytotoxic function of these cells.
Aim: This project aims to develop cytokine activated TGFBR2 knockout NK cells with enhanced antitumor activity for control cancer progression and metastasis.

NK cells will be engineered by CRISPR/Cas9 technology to knockout the TGFBR2 genes which will provide resistance to the inhibitory effect exerted by the TGF-β. TGFBR2 knockout NK cells will be activated with a complex of three cytokines in order to achieve their persistence and increased effector functions. NK cells engineered to express a substantial cytotoxic activity will be validated by testing on mouse models of melanoma.

OBJECTIVES and RESULTS

OBJECTIVES

O1. Generation of TGFBR2 knockout NK cells which will be activated with cytokines

O2. In vitro validation of enhanced antitumor activity of cytokine activated TGFBR2 knockout NK cells

O3. Validation of cytokine activated TGFBR2 knockout NK cells as a potential immunotherapeutic candidate for cancer therapy using mouse models of melanoma

RESULTS

An experimental model to overcome the limitation of NK cell cytotoxicity in tumour microenvironment by generating CRISPR-Cas9 engineered NK cells to knockout the TGF-β receptor 2 in order to become less sensitive to TGF-β.
